name: Happy Families
description: Happy Families is a traditional British matching game, famously illustrated by John Tenniel. It is a progenitor to games like Go Fish and Authors. Players attempt to collect complete sets (families) of four characters by asking opponents for specific cards. If successful, they continue their turn; if not, the turn passes to the person asked.

overview.description: Happy Families is a traditional British matching game, famously illustrated by John Tenniel. It is a progenitor to games like Go Fish and Authors. Players attempt to collect complete sets (families) of four characters by asking opponents for specific cards. If successful, they continue their turn; if not, the turn passes to the person asked.

history.origins: First published in 1851 by Jaques of London, the game featured characters who have since become iconic in British culture, such as 'Master Bun the Baker' and 'Mr. Dose the Doctor'.
timeline: 1851: Created by Jaques of London for the Great Exhibition.
Late 19th Century: Becomes a staple household game throughout the British Empire.
Modern Era: Influences the creation of Go Fish and Quartets globally.
history.cultural: Used idiomatically in Britain to describe a perfect-looking family unit.
history.evolution: The game has seen hundreds of thematic re-skins, ranging from educational subjects to pop culture characters, while the rules remains unchanged.

setup.deck: 44 characters divided into 11 families of 4 (Father, Mother, Son, Daughter).
setup.dealing: Deal all cards face-down to all players. Some players may have one more card than others; this is acceptable.

rules.objective: Collect and declare the highest number of complete families (sets of four).
rules.gameplay:
1. Player to the dealer's left starts.
2. ASKING: On your turn, ask a specific opponent for a specific card of a family you already hold at least one card of (e.g., 'Do you have Master Bun the Baker's Son?').
3. RESULT: If they have it, they give it to you and you continue asking anyone for another card. If they don't have it, they say 'Not at home!' and your turn ends. The player who was asked now begins their turn.
4. COMPLETION: When you collect all four members of a family, you must immediately lay them face-up on the table.
keyRules: You MUST hold at least one card of the family you are asking for.
You must ask for a SPECIFIC card (e.g., 'Master Bun the Baker's Daughter'), not just a general family.
A turn continues as long as you successfully receive requested cards.
The game ends when all families are completed.

strategy.basic: Remember which players asked for which families. If someone asks for a 'Bun' card, they hold at least one.
strategy.intermediate: If you are asked for a card you don't have, pay close attention to where that card eventually surfaces. Track which families are 'active' at the table.
strategy.advanced: Deduction: If Player A asks Player B for a card and Player B doesn't have it, you can safely assume Player C holds it if you don't have it yourself.
tips: Try to complete families you already have three of quickly before others guess your hand.
Watch for players who have few cards left; they are close to completing sets.
Listen to the 'Not at home' responses - they tell you who DOESN'T have a card just as much as a 'Yes' tells you who does.

variations.name: Quartets
variations.description: A European variant using a similar 32-card deck (8 sets of 4) often with educational themes like animals or cars.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Quartets differs mainly in deck size and theme; no engine overrides documented in sources.

scoring.description: Each completed family counts as one point.
scoring.winCondition: Player with the most points (families) wins.

synthesis.shortDescription: A classic memory and matching game where players ask for family members to build complete four-card sets. Success keeps your turn alive!
